On one B200, LFM2.5-1.2B on RIPL showed 14.4 to 28.4x lower p95 latency than Qwen3.5-0.8B on vLLM. The post Liquid AI Launches RIPL, a Real-Time Inference Engine for Sub-50 ms LFMs appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Liquid AI just announced Liquid RIPL , short for Real-time Inference Pipeline. RIPL is a low-latency engine that serves Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) inside a live request path. It returns complete generated responses end-to-end in under 50 ms. It also claims that latency holds while traffic arrives continuously at peak load. For developers, the message is simple. Swap gradient-boosted trees for a generative model, and keep the latency budget. TL;DR Engine : Serves LFM2.5 models from 230M to 2.6B parameters Runs on: Enterprise deployments on NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Benchmarks used a single B200. Performance: 5.6 to 28.4x lower p95 latency than Qwen3.5 on vLLM, per Liquid’s own tests. Best: LFM2.5-1.2B hit 155.8 ms p95 vs 4,431 ms for Qwen3.5-0.8B, a 28.4x gap (256 in, 128 out). Worst: LFM2.5-2.6B gained only 5.6x (449.1 ms vs 2,499 ms). Sub-50 ms fails on longer requests. What problem does Liquid RIPL solve? Most serving stacks target large batches and long agentic jobs. A few seconds per request is acceptable there. Search ranking, fraud checks and payment authorization need answers in milliseconds. Liquid AI argues teams default to classical models for these paths because LLM serving is too slow. RIPL is built to remove that trade-off. How does RIPL work? Liquid AI describes RIPL as optimizing the full path, from request arrival to completed response. In several workloads, Liquid AI plots the same model, LFM2.5-350M, on vLLM and on RIPL. RIPL’s p95 line sits well below the vLLM line in each case. That isolates part of the gain to the engine, not just the model architecture. The LFM2.5 models themselves are hybrids. LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct has 16 layers: 10 double-gated convolution blocks and 6 GQA blocks. LFM2.5-2.6B has 30 layers: 22 convolution blocks and 8 GQA blocks. RIPL benchmarks: how fast is it vs vLLM? Liquid measured p95 end-to-end latency under open-loop Poisson arrivals on one B200. LFMs ran on RIPL. Baselines, including MiniCPM5 and Granite 4.2, ran on vLLM. Workload Load LFM2.5 on RIPL (p95) Qwen3.5 on vLLM (p95) Gap 1B class, 32 in → 32 out 1,000 req/s 34.6 ms (1.2B) 498 ms (0.8B) 14.4x 1B class, 256 in → 128 out 400 req/s 155.8 ms (1.2B) 4,431 ms (0.8B) 28.4x 2B class, 32 in → 32 out 1,000 req/s 76.4 ms (2.6B) 586.8 ms (2B) 7.7x 2B class, 256 in → 128 out 300 req/s 449.1 ms (2.6B) 2,499 ms (2B) 5.6x Source: Liquid AI blog, Figure 2 . Sealf-reported. Liquid AI also mapped 6 real-time workloads against fixed budgets: Adtech query rewriting: 32 in, 32 out, 50 ms budget, LFM2.5-350M. Search intent classification: 128 in, 1 out, 20 ms budget. Search reranking: 1k in, 1 out, 30 ms budget. Payments risk scoring: 512 in, 16 out, 50 ms budget, LFM2.5-1.2B. Credit decisioning: 8k in, 64 out, 150 ms budget. Image alt text: 512×512 image and 64 tokens in, 16 out, 100 ms budget, LFM2.5-VL-450M . Yes, according to Liquid AI. Shopify is deploying LFMs across latency-sensitive commerce workloads. In search enhancement, LFMs run with sub-20 ms inference on production traffic. According to Liquid AI’s blog, they use about 50% fewer parameters than alternatives and deliver 2 to 10x faster inference. Key Takeaways RIPL is Liquid AI’s engine for LLMs inside live request paths. Liquid claims 5.6 to 28.4x lower p95 latency than Qwen3.5 on vLLM. Same-model tests (LFM2.5-350M) show RIPL itself beats vLLM. Shopify runs LFMs at sub-20 ms in production search. Enterprise-only, closed, and all figures are self-reported. The post Gradium Open-Sources Phonon, a 31M-Parameter On-Device TTS Model Under Apache 2.0 appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Gradium has open-sourced Phonon , a family of small text-to-speech models built to run on the device. The Gradium Phonon on-device TTS model comes in 31M and 40M sizes. The English Phonon 31m ships under Apache 2.0 and fits in a 64.5 MB file. Developers get natural speech with no cloud call, no GPU and no per-character bill. TL;DR Size: 31M parameters (excluding the audio tokenizer), 64.5 MB q8 GGUF, 24 kHz mono output. Phonon 40m: 40M, 74.6 MB. Runs on: CPUs, phones, Raspberry Pi 5, browsers (WASM, WebGPU) and NVIDIA GPUs. No GPU required. Performance: top English Elo among open models Gradium tested; about 7 ms to first audio on CPU. Best: 1.70% WER on a 500-sentence hard set, versus 3.50% for Kokoro (Gradium’s eval). Worst: 0.51% Seed-TTS LLM WER, behind Kokoro (0.45%) and Magpie (0.46%). What is Gradium Phonon? Phonon is an open-weight TTS family from Gradium , a Paris voice AI company spun out of Kyutai. It generates speech locally on phones, laptops, boards and browsers. The family has three models : Phonon 31m: English only, 37 built-in voices, Apache 2.0. Phonon 40m: 1 model per language (English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese), CC BY-NC 4.0. Phonon 40m multilingual: all 5 languages in 1 model, 102 voices, CC BY-NC 4.0. How does Phonon work? Phonon uses a causal transformer backbone. Its prefix combines text and speaker embeddings. A SentencePiece tokenizer with a 4,000-token vocabulary reads raw text, with no phoneme conversion. The backbone generates 1 latent vector per 80 ms frame. A flow-matching head turns that vector plus noise into an audio embedding in a single step. A smaller variant of Kyutai’s Mimi decoder then outputs 24 kHz PCM audio. A separate end-of-speech head decides when to stop. Phonon 31m uses 6 transformer layers, width 512 and 8 attention heads.
